blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — sucralfate local protective action
stem: Which statement best explains how sucralfate helps an active duodenal ulcer?

options.A: It acts locally by forming an ulcer-adherent complex that covers the ulcer surface and helps protect it from acid, pepsin, and bile salts.
options.B: It suppresses gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the parietal-cell proton pump and producing sustained acid suppression.
options.C: It increases upper gastrointestinal motility through dopamine-2 receptor antagonism, thereby accelerating gastric emptying and transit.
options.D: It reduces gastric acid secretion by blocking histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells and decreasing basal and stimulated acid output.

rationale: Current sucralfate labeling states that the drug is only minimally absorbed and exerts its effect through local rather than systemic action. It forms an ulcer-adherent complex with proteinaceous exudate at the ulcer site; the resulting barrier helps protect the ulcer against further attack by acid, pepsin, and bile salts. Therefore A is correct. B describes proton-pump inhibition, C describes a prokinetic dopamine-2 antagonist mechanism, and D describes H2-receptor blockade; none is the labeled mechanism of sucralfate.
educational_objective: Explain that sucralfate acts locally by adhering to the ulcer site and forming a protective barrier against acid, pepsin, and bile salts.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA labeling
source_locator: Clinical Pharmacology — minimal gastrointestinal absorption; local rather than systemic action; ulcer-adherent complex; barrier against acid, pepsin, and bile salts. Indications and Usage — active duodenal ulcer.
source_claim_supported: Sucralfate is minimally absorbed, acts locally, forms an ulcer-adherent complex at the ulcer site, and helps protect the ulcer from acid, pepsin, and bile salts; it is indicated for short-term treatment of active duodenal ulcer.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: educate client about medications; review pertinent data prior to medication administration; evaluate client response to medication.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as substantive gastrointestinal drug mechanisms of closely matched length.
Retained a single mechanism directly supported by the current sucralfate label and removed the original answer-length cue.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches current sucralfate Clinical Pharmacology and the active-duodenal-ulcer construct. B–D are plausible mechanisms of other GI therapies, all options are effectively length-matched, and no second defensible answer or cue remains.
